newsitem.title: KENYA: Sudan, rebels disagree on resuming peace talks.
newsitem.headline: Sudan, rebels disagree on resuming peace talks.

text.p: Sudan's president and its main rebel group disagreed on Wednesday on whether Khartoum accepting a framework for negotiations cleared the way for resumed talks to end 14 years of civil war.
Sudanese President Lieutenant-General Omar Hassan al-Bashir said the framework, "the declaration of principles", was not binding. A summit of regional leaders described it as a basis for discussion.

In response, a spokesman for the main Sudanese rebel group, the Sudan People's Liberation Army (SPLA), told Reuters it could not resume negotiations with Bashir after a break of nearly three years unless the framework was binding on both parties.

"If anyone is serious to bring peace to Sudan he can commit himself to the declaration of principles and that should be binding and the outcome of the negotiations should be binding," said SPLA spokesman George Maker Benjamin in Nairobi.
"We will not go to talks if Bashir sticks to his position that the declaration of principles is not binding," he added.
Talks in Nairobi between Bashir and SPLA leader John Garang mediated by regional states broke down in September 1994 when Khartoum refused to sign the declaration of principles after the rebels had.

The leaders of Kenya, Ethiopia, Eritrea, Sudan and Djibouti and a representative of Uganda earlier on Wednesday hailed the Sudanese acceptance of the declaration of principles as "a major breakthrough" in the long search for peace in southern Sudan.
"The summit welcomed the acceptance by the government of Sudan of the declaration of principles as the basis for discussions and negotiations," the leaders said at the end of a two-day summit.
"This will enable the parties to the conflict to freely discuss and negotiate on all the points enshrined in the declaration of principles," they added in the statement.
But at a news conference Bashir said Khartoum refused to sign the declaration of principles in 1994 as at that time it was understood they were obligatory and binding on both sides.
The declaration included the separation of religion and the state and the principle of self-determination for south Sudan.
"Now following intensive consultations and deliberations by the summit, this thing has been redefined as a basis for negotiations and discussion," said the Sudanese president.
Garang, because he was not a head of state, was not invited to the summit but has been in Nairobi for the past five days in case the five leaders wanted to consult him on their talks.
Benjamin said the SPLA believed resuming peace talks between Bashir and Garang would merely "be a public relations exercise" unless Khartoum was committed to the declaration of principles.
The summit, which ended on Wednesday, called on Kenya's President Daniel arap Moi to arrange a speedy resumption of the talks under the Inter-Governmental Authority on Development.

"The summit called on the parties to the conflict to create the conducive environment necessary for the resumption of negotiations," said the leaders and a representative of Ugandan President Yoweri Museveni, who failed to attend the summit.
The Nairobi summit made little progress on the problem of seven years of civil war in Somalia, which was also discussed.

"The summit noted with grave concern that peace in Somalia remains elusive," said the leaders, who however encouraged southern Somali factions to attend a national reconciliation conference called for November by an Ethiopian-backed alliance.
Somali faction leader Hussein Aideed, based in southern Mogadishu, refuses to attend the talks in northeast Somalia.
